In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Hujurat

Al-Mahayimi said: It was named after this, because the meaning of its first verse indicates the stripping of humanity from anyone who does not venerate the Messenger of God to the utmost degree of veneration and does not honour him to the utmost degree of honour. This is one of the greatest aims of the Qur'an.

It is a Medinan surah, and its verses number eighteen.

This surah is distinguished by noble etiquette, through which God educated His believing servants in how they should treat His Prophet (ﷺ), in terms of reverence and exaltation.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Discourse on the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words:

[1] ﴿O you who have believed, do not put yourselves forward before God and His Messenger, and fear God. Indeed, God is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, do not put yourselves forward before God and His Messenger﴾. Ibn Jarir said: That is, O you who have affirmed the oneness of God and the prophethood of His Prophet (ﷺ), do not hasten to decide a matter in your wars or your religion before God and His Messenger have decided it for you, lest you decide contrary to the command of God and the command of His Messenger. It is related from the Arabs: "So-and-so puts himself forward before his imam", meaning he hastens to issue an order or prohibition without him. End of quote.

And: ﴿tuqaddimu﴾ is either transitive with its object omitted, because the generality is intended, or it is treated as intransitive because no object is intended, as you say: "So-and-so gives and withholds." Or it is intransitive, for qaddama may come with the meaning of taqaddama, like bayyana, which is transitive and becomes intransitive with the meaning of tabayyana.

In this sentence there are two figurative usages:

The first concerns "between the two hands" (bayn al-yadayn). Its literal meaning is the space between the two limbs, and so the phrase was used figuratively for the two directions opposite the right and the left, approximately by applying the term "two hands" to what borders them and faces them. This is metonymy of the general kind (al-majaz al-mursal). Then the whole sentence was used as a metaphorical image (isti'arah tamthiliyyah) for asserting a ruling without following or obeying those whom one is obliged to follow, depicting its ugliness and monstrousness in the form of something sensible, like a servant walking ahead of his master on a journey. So the first expression, with the figurative usage it contains, was transferred to what has been mentioned, as is known of similar cases. This is the essence of what is in al-Kashshaf (the Kashshaf) and its commentaries.

(Ibn Kathir said: The meaning of the verse is: do not be hasty in matters before Him, but be followers of Him in all affairs, so that the hadith of Mu'adh, may God be pleased with him, enters under the generality of this etiquette. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him when he sent him to Yemen: "By what will you judge?" He said: "By the Book of God, the Exalted." He (ﷺ) said: "And if you do not find it?" He said: "By the Sunnah of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." He (ﷺ) said: "And if you do not find it?" He said, may God be pleased with him: "I will exercise my own opinion (ijtihad, independent reasoning)!" So he struck him on the chest and said: "Praise be to God who has granted success to the messenger of the Messenger of God in what pleases the Messenger of God." This was related by Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah. The point of it is that he deferred his opinion, his consideration and his effort (ijtihad) until after the Book and the Sunnah. Had he put it forward before searching in them, it would have been a case of putting oneself forward before God and His Messenger. End of quote.)

It has been permitted that the intended meaning is "before the Messenger of God", and God was mentioned to show the strength of his being specially connected to Him, and his high station with Him, as a preparation and introduction for what follows. This has been supported by the argument that the context of the speech is for the exaltation of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Note:

Ibn Jarir said: With a damma on the ta' in His words "do not put forward" (la tuqaddimu), he recited the recitation of the cities (qira'at al-amsar), which is the recitation I do not permit reciting contrary to, because of the consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement) of the authoritative reciters upon it. It has been related from the Arabs: qaddamtu fi kadha and taqaddamtu fi kadha (I put forward in such-and-such). On this usage, had it been said "la taqaddamu" with a fatha on the ta', it would have been permissible. End of quote. And with this Ya'qub recited, as is transmitted from him.

﴿And fear God﴾, that is: regarding putting forward or opposing the ruling. The command to fear God comes right after what preceded, and is like your saying to someone who has committed some offence: "Do not do this, and guard against what brings shame upon you." You first forbid him from the very thing he committed, then you generalise and command him with what, if he had obeyed your command in it, he would not have committed that heedlessness, nor any of what leads to it and is connected to its cause. Al-Zamakhshari pointed this out.

﴿Indeed, God is Hearing and Knowing﴾, that is: therefore He is worthy to be feared and to be watched over.

Note:

In al-Iklil: Al-Kiya al-Harrasi said: It was said that it was revealed concerning a people who slaughtered before the Prophet (ﷺ), so he ordered them to repeat the slaughter. The general implication of the verse is the prohibition of hastening in command and prohibition ahead of him. The verse is used as evidence for following the Sharia in everything. Those who deny analogical reasoning (qiyas) have sometimes used it as evidence, and this is false on their part. It is also used as evidence for giving precedence to the text over analogical reasoning. End of quote.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[2] ﴿O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, and do not speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another, lest your deeds be nullified while you are unaware.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾ That is: when he speaks and you speak, your voices should fall short of the level that his voice reaches, so that his voice stays higher than your speech. Do not drown out his voice with your noise, or let your voices reach the ears of those present before his voice does. Doing so is a great breach of etiquette. ﴿And do not speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another﴾ That is: rather, in addressing him, deliberately use gentle speech, close to a whisper, which is the opposite of loud speech, as one addresses someone who is held in awe and esteem. It is narrated from Mujahid that it means calling him by his name, that is, do not call out to him as some of you call to others: "O Muhammad! O Muhammad!" Rather say: "O Prophet of God! O Messenger of God!" The commentators of the (Kashshaf) (al-Zamakhshari's tafsir) have objected to this, saying that mentioning loud speech in this context has no apparent sense, since the obvious wording would be: "Do not make your address to him like the address of some of you to others," as was stated in His saying: ﴿Do not make the summoning of the Messenger among yourselves like the summoning of some of you by others﴾ [al-Nur: 63]. End of quote.

You may say: this meaning narrated from Mujahid was cast in that noble expression because of the Qur'an's practice of choosing the most delicate and refined words and sentences in such matters. Its style is above every style. He also said: "If the tafsir from Mujahid reaches you, it is enough for you." ﴿lest your deeds be nullified﴾ That is: for fear that your deeds will be nullified by raising your voices above his voice, and by speaking loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another. ﴿while you are unaware﴾ That is: you do not know, and are not aware, that they are being nullified.

Note:

The Mu'tazila (a theological school) used this verse as evidence that major sins nullify deeds, since what is mentioned in the verse is a major sin that nullifies, with no distinction between it and other sins. But since, according to the Ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni majority), the only thing that nullifies deeds is specifically disbelief (kufr), they interpreted the verse as a matter of severe warning and intimidation, since it was placed in the rank of nullifying disbelief. Or it is an allusion to the hypocrites who intend, by raising their voices and speaking loudly, to show contempt. Their action is certainly nullified.

Al-Nasir (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: the verse means a prohibition of raising the voice absolutely. It is known that the ruling of a prohibition is caution against what is feared in it of harming the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. The accepted principle is that harming him, peace and blessings be upon him, reaches the level of disbelief that nullifies deeds, by agreement. So a prohibition came concerning what is likely to cause harm to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, whether or not that meaning exists, as a safeguard against the means (dhari'a) and to cut off the root. Then, since this forbidden act, raising the voice, divides into what reaches that level from the outset and what does not, and there is no evidence distinguishing one of the two parts from the other, the responsible person must refrain from it entirely, and he is warned lest he fall into what nullifies the deed, namely what reaches the point of harm, since there is no clear evidence that distinguishes it. Even if there were, its distinction would often not be achieved. It is to the confusion of one part with the other that the allusion is made by His saying: ﴿lest your deeds be nullified while you are unaware﴾. Otherwise, if the matter were as the Mu'tazila believe, His saying ﴿while you are unaware﴾ would have no place. For the matter is between raising the voice being harmful, in which case it is certainly disbelief that nullifies, and its being non-harmful, in which case it is certainly a major sin that is nullified in their view. So in both of its states, nullification by it is established. Therefore there is no place for the sentence's ending with unawareness, although awareness is established absolutely, and God knows best.

Then he said: This explanation I have given rests on two premises, both of which are sound:

The first: raising the voice is of the kind of thing by which harm is caused. This is a matter attested by transmission and by present observation, to the point that a teacher is harmed by a student raising his voice before him. How much more so at the rank of prophethood and what it deserves of reverence and magnification.

The second premise: harming the Prophet ﷺ is disbelief. This is a settled matter, explicitly stated by our imams, meaning the Malikis, who issued rulings to kill anyone who committed it as an act of disbelief, and whose repentance is not accepted. What he has done is greater and more grievous before God. And God is the one who grants success. End of quote.

It should not be hidden that fairness lies in standing by what the text has made clear and manifest. Every place where nullification is explicitly stated must be accepted without interpretation, and analogy based on it is ruled out, because it is a context of threat and loss, and there is no room for opinion in such a matter. This is what I hold and what I think. God speaks the truth, and He guides to the right way.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 49, verse 3:

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[3] ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah — those are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety. For them is forgiveness and a great reward.﴾

﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices﴾, that is: those who go to great lengths in lowering them. ﴿In the presence of the Messenger of Allah — those are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety﴾. Ibn Jarir said: that is, He has chosen them and purified them for piety (p-5443), meaning for their being God-fearing through performing His obedience and avoiding His disobediences, just as gold is tested by fire, so that its good part is purified and its impurity is eliminated. ﴿For them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾, that is: abundant reward, which is Paradise.

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 49, verse 4:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[4] ﴿Indeed, those who call you from behind the chambers—most of them do not use reason.﴾

﴿Indeed, those who call you﴾, i.e., who summon you; ﴿from behind﴾, i.e., from outside; ﴿the chambers﴾, i.e., while you are within them, in haste for your coming out to them, even if that means abandoning what you are occupied with of affairs; ﴿most of them do not use reason﴾, since such conduct is not done by one who is modest, nor is it done to a modest person, so they do not observe the sanctity of their own selves, nor your sanctity. It is attributed to the majority, because a person of intellect may follow a group of the ignorant, in agreement with them.

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[5] ﴿And if they had patiently waited until you came out to them, it would have been better for them. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

﴿And if they had patiently waited until you came out to them, it would have been better for them﴾ That is: because your coming out in response to their haste may anger him, and they would miss the benefits of seeing him and hearing his speech. But if they had been patient, they would have gained many benefits, along with their being characterized by patience and by preserving the sanctity of their Prophet and of themselves. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ That is: to whoever repents of disobedience to Allah, by calling out to you in this manner, and returns to Allah's command regarding it and regarding other matters.

Remarks:

The first: Ibn Kathir said: It has been mentioned that it was revealed concerning al-Aqra' ibn Habis al-Tamimi, as related by more than one narrator.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman, from al-Aqra' ibn Habis, that he called out to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying: "O Muhammad! O Muhammad!" - (and in another narration: "O Messenger of Allah!") - but he did not answer him. He said: "O Messenger of Allah! Indeed my praise is an adornment, and indeed my blame is a disgrace." He said: "That is Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Ibn Ishaq narrated, in the mention of the year nine, which is called the Year of Delegations: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ conquered Makkah, finished with Tabuk, and Thaqif had embraced Islam and pledged allegiance, the delegations of the Arabs came to him from every direction. Among them was the delegation of Banu Tamim. When they entered the mosque, they called out to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from behind his chambers: 'Come out to us, O Muhammad!' This harmed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ because of their shouting, so he came out to them." Then Ibn Ishaq related their account at length, then said: And concerning them there was revealed from the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers, most of them do not reason﴾ [al-Hujurat: 4].

The second: "al-Hujurat" (الحُجُرات) is read with two dammas, with a fatha on the jim, and with a sukun on it; all of these readings are recited, and it is the plural of "hujrah" (حُجْرَة), which is a plot of land enclosed by a wall surrounding it. It is of the form fu'lah in the sense of maf'ulah, like "ghurfah" and "qubdah."

Al-Zamakhshari said: The intended meaning is the chambers of the wives of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and each of them had a chamber. Their calling out to him from behind them may mean that they had dispersed among the chambers seeking him, so one of them called out from behind this one and another from behind that one, or that they came to them chamber by chamber and called out to him from behind them, or that they called out to him from behind the chamber in which he was. But it was given in the plural out of honor for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and due to the place of his sanctity. And the act, although attributed to all of them, may be carried out by some of them while the rest were content, so it is as though they all carried it out.

The third: Al-Zamakhshari said: The revelation of the verse in the manner in which it came contains, among its clear evidences of magnifying the station of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and honoring him, what is not hidden from the observer:

Among them: its coming in the rhyming form which brands those who shouted with it with foolishness and ignorance for what they undertook.

Among them: the word "al-hujurat" and its use, as a metonymy for the place of his seclusion and resting with some of his wives.

Among them: passing over its wording, limiting oneself to the extent by which what was condemned of them is made clear.

Among them: the definite article being used rather than an annexation.

Among them: that it paired their blame with their rudeness, the weakness of their reasoning, and their poor discernment of the proper places for distinction in addressing, to lighten the matter upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, to console him, and to remove what entered him of the distress of their boorishness and bad manners, and so on... from the beginning of the surah to the end of this verse. So consider how it began by making obligatory that matters which belong to Allah and His Messenger be given precedence over all matters, without restriction or qualification. Then it followed that prohibition with what is of the same kind as precedence, namely raising the voice and speaking loudly, as though the first was the groundwork for the second and a preparation for its mention. Then it mentioned what is praise of those who avoided that and lowered their voices, indicating the great standing of the Prophet with Allah. Then, immediately after that, came what is more grave and whose ugliness is more complete: shouting at the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was in seclusion with some of his sanctities, from behind the walls, as one shouts at the least of people in rank, to alert to the enormity of what they brought about and dared to do. For whoever Allah has elevated in rank above being addressed loudly, such that the foremost of the Muhajirun and the Ansar addressed him as "brother of secrecy," the conduct of these people was of the reprehensible kind that reached an extreme of indecency. From this and similar things the fruit of minds is gathered and the beauties of manners are drawn out, as is related from Abu Ubayd, whose standing in knowledge, asceticism, and trustworthiness of narration is not hidden, that he said: "I never knocked on the door of a scholar, ever, until he came out at the time of his coming out." End.

The fourth: Ibn Kathir said: The scholars said: It is disliked to raise the voice at his grave ﷺ, as it was disliked during his life, for he is honored both alive and in his grave ﷺ. It has been transmitted to us from the Commander of the Faithful Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he heard the voices of two men in the Mosque of the Prophet ﷺ whose voices had risen, so he pelted them with pebbles. Then he called them and said: "From where are you two?" They said: "From the people of al-Ta'if." He said: "If you were from the people of Madinah, I would have struck you painfully." End.

The fifth: Al-Bukhari narrated from Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr that "a riding party from Banu Tamim came to the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Bakr said: 'Appoint al-Qa'qa' ibn Ma'bad,' and Umar said: 'Appoint al-Aqra' ibn Habis.' Abu Bakr said: 'You only intended to oppose me!' Umar said: 'I did not intend to oppose you!' So they disputed until their voices rose. Thereupon it was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put [yourselves] before Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Hujurat: 1] until the verse ended.

In another narration: Then Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿O you who have believed, do not raise your voices﴾ [al-Hujurat: 2], the verse.

Ibn al-Zubayr said: After this verse, Umar would not speak to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ except in a manner of asking him to repeat." Al-Bukhari alone narrated these two narrations without Muslim.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said: This has raised a difficulty! Ibn Atiyyah said: The correct view is that the cause of revelation of this verse was the speech of rough Bedouins.

Ibn Hajar said: I say: this does not contradict that hadith, for what relates to the story of the two shaykhs in their disagreement over appointment is the beginning of the surah: ﴿do not put forward﴾ [al-Hujurat: 1]. But when his saying ﴿do not raise﴾ [al-Hujurat: 2] was joined to it, Umar took from it the lowering of his voice. The rough Bedouins about whom it was revealed are from Banu Tamim, and it is specifically about them, and His saying ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 4]. End.

We have previously, many times, given the answer to similar cases: that the saying "this verse was revealed concerning such-and-such" may mean that it is cited as evidence that something similar falls under the verse, not that it was the cause of its revelation.

Imam Ibn Taymiyyah said: Their saying "this verse was revealed concerning such-and-such" is sometimes meant as the cause of revelation, and sometimes meant as that this matter is included in the verse even if it was not the cause, as you say: "by this verse he meant such-and-such." End.

By this is answered what many narrate concerning the multiplicity of causes of revelation, so keep this in mind, for it is among what is guarded from those who are not its people. Had Ibn Atiyyah examined this, he would not have weakened the narration of al-Bukhari, nor would Ibn Hajar have strained to split the verses by assigning some to one cause and others to another within a single story. And success is from Allah. And the saying of His Exalted:

The commentary on the words of Allah, Exalted is He:

[6] ﴿O you who have believed, if a deviator brings you a report, verify it, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and then become, over what you have done, regretful.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, if a deviator brings you a report, verify it﴾ means: seek to establish its truth from its falsehood by another means. ﴿Lest you harm a people out of ignorance﴾ means: a people innocent of what they have been accused of, intending to harm them, out of ignorance of their deserving it. Then it becomes clear to you that they did not deserve it. ﴿And then become, over what you have done, regretful﴾ means: you will regret having afflicted them with the wrongdoing you inflict upon them. It is incumbent upon the believer to guard against that which he fears will cause him regret in its consequences.

Notes:

First: Ibn Kathir said: Many of the exegetes mention that this verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent him to collect the alms of Banu al-Mustaliq. This has been related through several chains, and among the best of them is what Imam Ahmad related in his Musnad through the narration of Malik from Ibn al-Mustaliq, who is al-Harith ibn Dirar, father of Juwayriyah, Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her. Imam Ahmad said: Muhammad ibn Sabiq narrated to us, 'Isa ibn Dinar narrated to us, my father narrated to me that he heard al-Harith ibn Dirar al-Khuza'i, may Allah be pleased with him, say: "I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he invited me to Islam, so I entered it and affirmed it, and he invited me to zakat, so I affirmed it and said: O Messenger of Allah! I will return to my people and call them to Islam and to paying zakat. Whoever responds to me, I will gather his zakat, and send to me, O Messenger of Allah, a messenger at such and such a time, so that he may come to you with what I have gathered of zakat."

When al-Harith gathered the zakat from those who responded to him, and the appointed time came when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ intended to send to him, the messenger was delayed and did not come to him. al-Harith thought that there had been displeasure against him from Allah and His Messenger. So he summoned the chiefs of his people and said to them: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had set a time for me, when he would send his messenger to collect what I had of zakat. The Messenger of Allah does not break his promise, and I do not think that the delay of his messenger is anything but due to displeasure. So come, let us go to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent al-Walid ibn Uqbah to al-Harith to collect what he had gathered of zakat. When al-Walid set out and reached part of the way, he became fearful, so he returned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah! al-Harith withheld the zakat from me and intended to kill me." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then dispatched a force to al-Harith.

Al-Harith came out with his companions, and when he met the force, having left Medina, they said: "This is al-Harith!" When he reached them, he said to them: "To whom have you been sent?" They said: "To you." He said: "Why?" They said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had sent al-Walid ibn Uqbah to you, and he claimed that you withheld zakat from him and intended to kill him!" He said: "No, by the One who sent Muhammad with the truth, I did not see him at all, and he did not come to me." When al-Harith entered upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he said: "You withheld zakat and intended to kill my messenger?!" He said: "No, by the One who sent you with the truth! I did not see him at all, and he did not come to me. I only came when the messenger of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was delayed for me. I feared that there had been displeasure from Allah and His Messenger." Then the Hujurat was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, if a deviator brings you a report﴾ up to His words: ﴿Wise﴾ [al-Hujurat: 8]."

Mujahid and Qatadah said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent al-Walid ibn Uqbah to Banu al-Mustaliq to collect their charity. They met him with the charity, but he returned and said: 'Banu al-Mustaliq have gathered against you to fight you' (Qatadah added: 'and they have apostatized from Islam'). So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Khalid ibn al-Walid, may Allah be pleased with him, to them, and instructed him to verify and not to hasten. He set out until he came to them at night, and sent his scouts. When they came back, they informed Khalid, may Allah be pleased with him, that they were steadfast in Islam, and that they heard their call to prayer and their prayer. When morning came, Khalid, may Allah be pleased with him, came to them and saw what pleased him. He returned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and informed him of the news, and Allah, Exalted is He, revealed this verse." Qatadah said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say: 'Verification is from Allah, and haste is from Shaytan.'" Likewise, other than one of the early scholars mentioned, including Ibn Abi Layla, Yazid ibn Ruman, al-Dahhak, Muqatil and others, that this verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn Uqbah, and Allah knows best. End of quotation.

Ibn Qutaybah said in al-Ma'arif: al-Walid ibn Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt ibn Abi 'Amr ibn Umayyah ibn Abd Shams, and he was the maternal brother of Uthman, his mother being Arwa bint Kurayz. He embraced Islam on the day of the conquest of Makkah, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent him as a collector of charity to Banu al-Mustaliq. He went to them and said: "They withheld charity from me!" He was lying, so Allah revealed this verse. Umar appointed him over the charity of Banu Taghlib, and Uthman appointed him over Kufa after Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. He led the people of Kufa in the dawn prayer while intoxicated, four rak'ahs, and said: "Shall I add more for you?" They testified against him for drinking wine in the presence of Uthman, and he dismissed him alone. He remained in Medina until Ali was given allegiance, then he went out to al-Raqqa, settled there, and withdrew from both Ali and Mu'awiyah. He died in the region of al-Raqqa.

Second: In al-Iklil: The verse contains the rejection of the report of a deviator and the requirement of uprightness (adalah) in the one who reports, whether a narrator, a witness, or a jurist. The verse is used as evidence for the acceptance of the report of a single trustworthy person. Ibn Kathir said: From here, groups of scholars refrained from accepting the narration of one whose state is unknown, due to the possibility of his being a deviator in reality; and others accepted it, because we are only commanded to verify when the report is from a deviator, and this one is not certainly a deviator, since his state is unknown.

Third: Regarding the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿and then become, over what you have done, regretful﴾, there are two benefits:

The first: affirming and emphasizing the warning. Its reasoning is that when Allah, Exalted is He, said ﴿lest you harm a people out of ignorance﴾, He then said: this is not something to be disregarded, and it is not permissible for a sensible person to say: "Suppose I harmed a people, what would be upon me?" Rather, upon you from it is constant concern and lasting grief. Such a matter is obligatory to guard against.

The second: praise of the believers, i.e., you are not (such that), al-Mahayimi said: when they commit an evil, they do not heed it, but rather you become regretful over it. (Reported by al-Razi.)

The discourse on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[7] ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah. Were he to obey you in many matters, you would surely be in hardship. But Allah has endeared faith to you and made it beautiful in your hearts, and made disbelief, wickedness and disobedience hateful to you. Those are the rightly guided.﴾

﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah.﴾ Ibn Jarir said: Exalted is His remembrance, says to the companions of the Prophet of Allah ﷺ: "And know, O believers in Allah and His Messenger, that among you is the Messenger of Allah. So fear Allah lest you speak falsehood and fabricate lies, for Allah informs him of your affairs, makes known to him your news, and keeps him upright in his affairs."

﴿Were he to obey you in many matters, you would surely be in hardship.﴾ Al-Tabari said: That is, if the Messenger of Allah ﷺ were to act in matters according to your opinions and accept from you what you say to him, thereby obeying you, hardship (ʿanat), meaning severity and difficulty, would befall you in many matters through his obeying you, had he obeyed you, because he would err in his actions. Such as when he accepted from al-Walid ibn ʿUqba his statement concerning Banu al-Mustaliq, that they had apostatized, withheld the zakat, and gathered forces to fight the Muslims. So he (the Prophet) attacked them, killing some of them and taking some of their blood and property, whereas he had been wrong to kill and you (had been wrong) to kill those whom it was not lawful for him or for you to kill, and you took from the wealth what was not lawful for him or for you to take from the property of a Muslim people, and so hardship from Allah befell you because of that. And ʿanat means hardship, or ruin, or sin, or corruption.

Note:

The phrase (أنَّ) together with what is within its scope occupies the place of the two objects of (اعلموا, "know"). This is in view of the circumstantial clause restricted by it, which is His words: ﴿were he to obey you…﴾ etc., for it is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from the pronoun in the genitive in "fīkum" (among you) that is concealed within it. The meaning is: that he is among you in a state that requires changing, or that you are in a similar state, namely that you wish that he would follow you in many events, and if he did that you would fall into ignorance and ruin. In this there is an indication that some of them had embellished for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he should attack Banu al-Mustaliq, and that he did not obey their opinion in this. It is also permissible that ﴿Were he to obey you…﴾ be a new independent sentence. However, al-Zamakhshari rejected this possibility, saying: because it leads to discord in the composition, for if ﴿Were he to obey you…﴾ etc. were taken as a sentence in itself, the speech would not hold together in its parts, since there would then be no benefit in His words ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah﴾ when it is separated from what follows it. It was answered that it is permissible to intend by it an alert to the greatness of his position ﷺ, and that they, through their ignorance of his station, are negligent regarding the honour that is due to him, and regarding the fact that their duty is to follow him and not to follow their own opinions, as if they were unaware that he is among them. Thus it clarifies the permissibility of beginning a new sentence, and of pausing at ﴿the Messenger of Allah﴾.

﴿But Allah has endeared faith to you and made it beautiful in your hearts.﴾ That is: then how fitting it is for you to obey the Messenger of Allah and follow him, whereby Allah will protect you from hardship in what would befall you if you made the Messenger of Allah's opinion follow your opinion. ﴿And made disbelief hateful to you﴾, that is, in Allah. ﴿And wickedness﴾, meaning lying. ﴿And disobedience﴾, that is, opposing the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and neglecting what Allah has commanded. ﴿Those are…﴾, that is, those described by the love of faith and its adornment in their hearts, and their aversion to sins: ﴿the rightly guided﴾, that is, those who travel the path of truth.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[8] ﴿A bounty from Allah and favor; and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

﴿A bounty from Allah and favor﴾ means: a kindness from Him, and a favor He has bestowed upon you. Al-Qashani said: It is a bounty (fadl) by His solicitude for them in eternity, which entails the spiritual guidance of preparedness (al-hidayah al-ruhaniyyah al-isti'dadiyyah), which in turn entails these perfections in eternity. And it is a favor (ni'mah) through His enabling them to act in accordance with that original guidance, and His assistance by pouring out upon them the perfections suited to their preparedness, until they acquired the faculty of infallibility (malakat al-'ismah), which necessitates aversion to disobedience. This is an explanation (ta'lil) for "He made it beloved" (habbaba) and "He made it hateful" (karraha), and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad); or it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: that occurred as a bounty, or "they seek a bounty."

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾ means: possessing knowledge of the one who does good and the one who does evil, and wisdom in the management of His creation and in disposing them in what He wills of His decree.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 49, verse 9:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[9] ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, then make peace between them. But if one of them oppresses the other, then fight against the one that oppresses until it returns to the command of Allah. Then if it returns, make peace between them with justice and be equitable. Indeed, Allah loves those who are equitable.﴾

﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾, i.e., fight one another. ﴿Then make peace between them﴾. Ibn Jarir said: i.e., by calling them to the judgment of the Book of Allah and to acceptance of what is in it, for them and against them. That is the reconciliation between them with justice.

﴿But if one of them oppresses the other﴾, i.e., if one of these two groups refuses to respond to the judgment of the Book of Allah, for it or against it, and transgresses what Allah has made the standard of justice among His creation, while the other group of them responds. ﴿Then fight against the one that oppresses﴾, i.e., the one that transgresses and refuses to respond to the judgment of Allah. ﴿Until it returns to the command of Allah﴾, i.e., returns to the judgment of Allah which He has decreed in His Book among His creation. ﴿Then if it returns﴾, i.e., the transgressing group returns, after your fighting against them, to acceptance of the judgment of Allah in His Book. ﴿Then make peace between them with justice﴾, i.e., with fairness between them, and that is the judgment of Allah in His Book which He made the standard of justice among His creation. ﴿And be equitable﴾, i.e., be just in everything you do and leave undone. ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the equitable﴾, i.e., He will reward them with the best reward.

Notes:

First: Al-Qashani said: Fighting occurs only from inclination toward the world, reliance upon desire, attraction to the lower direction, and turning toward partial aims. Reconciliation comes only from adherence to justice in the soul, which is the shadow of love, which is the shadow of unity. Therefore the believers who affirm divine unity are commanded to make peace between them, on the assumption that they oppress one another, and to fight the oppressing group on the assumption that one of them oppresses, until it returns, because the oppressing group opposes the truth and repels it.

It has been narrated that this verse was revealed concerning two groups of al-Aws and al-Khazraj who fought over some matter in dispute, with sandals and hands, not with swords. This was reported to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he came to them, separated them, and reconciled them. This is related through many routes, which strengthens the view that the fighting in question was literal.

It is narrated from al-Hasan that "fighting" (iqtital) means dispute, and "fighting" (qital) means repelling, metaphorically. He said, as related by al-Tabari from him: There would be a dispute between two tribes, and he would call them to judgment, and they would refuse to respond, so Allah revealed: ﴿And if two groups﴾ up to His saying ﴿fight against the one that oppresses﴾, the verse. He says: push them toward judgment; their fighting was repelling. End of quote. It is not hidden that the root may be taken in its literal and metaphorical senses, so it encompasses both. The lexicographers have said: not every fighting is killing, and dispute may lead to killing. So there is no barrier to intending from the verse what is more general, so that the benefit is more comprehensive, and Allah knows best.

Second: In al-Iklil: the verse indicates the obligation of reconciliation between the people of justice and the people of oppression, and the fighting of the rebels, and this includes the people of Makkah as well as others; and that whoever returns from them and turns back is not to be fought, due to His saying: "until it returns." End of quote.

Sa'id related from Marwan who said: A crier shouted to Ali on the day of the Camel: Let no one who turns back be killed, let no wounded man be finished off, whoever closes his door is safe, and whoever lays down his weapon is safe.

The jurists have agreed on the prohibition of killing their fleeing and wounded, that their property is not taken as spoils, and their offspring are not taken captive, because they did not become disbelievers through their rebellion or their fighting. The inviolability of property follows their religion, and therefore what was taken from them must be returned to them. They are not liable for what they destroyed during the war, whether of life or property. Whoever among the people of rebellion is killed is washed, shrouded, and prayed over. But if a just person is killed, he is a martyr, so he is not washed or prayed over, because he was killed in fighting that Allah commanded, like the martyr of the battlefield against the disbelievers.

If a group manifests the opinion of the Kharijites, such as declaring disbelief in one who commits a major sin, abandoning the community, and considering the blood and property of Muslims lawful, and they do not gather for war, they are not to be targeted. If they commit a crime and incur a prescribed penalty, it is enforced upon them.

If two groups fight out of partisanship or a desire for leadership, then both are oppressors, because each of them is rebelling against the other, and each of them is liable for what it destroyed of the other's.

This is a fragment of what came in al-Iqna' and its commentary and its detailed treatment there.

Third: In Sharh al-Iqna' he said: In the verse there are benefits: among them, that they did not leave the faith through rebellion; that it made fighting them obligatory; that it removed from them liability for what they destroyed in fighting; and the permissibility of anyone who withholds a right owed to him. The hadiths on this are well known. Among them is what 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit narrated: "We pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to hear and obey, in ease and in hardship, and not to dispute the command with its people." Agreed upon. The Companions unanimously agreed on fighting them: Abu Bakr fought those who withheld zakat, and Ali fought the people of the Camel and the people of Siffin. End of quote.

The verse also indicates the obligation of assisting the one who is wronged, by His saying: "fight," and the obligation of offering sincere counsel, by His saying: ﴿then make peace between them﴾, and the striving for reconciliation, which is clear.

Fourth: The reason for the plural in "iqtatalu" (they fought), although it may be said that the apparent form would be "iqtatalata" (they two fought), is that it is the use of meaning over wording: since the two groups are in the sense of a people and folk. The point of taking the meaning first and then the wording is the reverse of what is common in usage. It has been said that initially, during the fighting, they are mixed and gathered together, so the pronoun is first pluralized; and during reconciliation they are distinct and separated, so the pronoun is made dual afterward. The secret of linking the second reconciliation with justice, but not the first, is that the second, occurring after fighting, is liable to suggest bearing harshly upon them with harm, or to give the impression that since they compelled them to fight, they deserve injustice from them.

Fifth: (aqsata), the quadriliteral, has its hamza for negation, i.e., remove injustice and be just. Unlike (qasata), the triliteral, whose meaning is to act unjustly. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And as for the unjust, they will be fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Jinn: 15]. This is the well-known usage, contrary to al-Zajjaj, who made the two equivalent; this was related by al-Karkhi. And the saying of Allah, exalted is He:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[10] ﴿The believers are but brothers, so make settlement between your two brothers and fear Allah, that you may receive mercy.﴾

﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ is a resumptive statement confirming what is contained in the command to reconcile, for it is among the necessary implications of brotherhood that they reconcile.

Al-Shihab said: Naming the sharing in faith "brotherhood" is an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh), or a metaphor (isti'arah) in which the sharing in faith is likened to sharing in the origin of descent, since each of them is a source of continuance, for procreation is the origin of life, and faith is the origin of everlasting survival in the Gardens.

﴿So make settlement between your two brothers﴾ means: if the two fight, then bring them to the judgment of Allah and the judgment of His Messenger.

Al-Qashani said: He, exalted is He, made clear that faith, the least of whose rank is monotheism and action, necessitates true brotherhood among the believers, owing to the original affinity and the natural kinship, which exceed the formal kinship and the filial relation by an incomparable degree, since it requires heartfelt love, not carnal love, which is caused by harmony in the fleshly bond. Therefore, at the very least, there is reconciliation, which is among the necessary implications of justice and one of its qualities. For if they had not deviated from the natural disposition, nor been clouded by the veils of their upbringing, they would not have fought or opposed one another. So it is obligatory upon the people of purity, in accordance with the requirement of mercy, compassion, and tenderness that are necessary to true brotherhood, to reconcile between the two and restore them to purity. End.

Note of caution:

Placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, with an addition to those commanded, is for emphasis in affirmation and specification. The mention of two alone, rather than the plural, is because the least number among whom discord occurs is two. So when reconciliation is required between the fewest, it is all the more required among the many, for corruption in the discord of a group is greater than in the discord of two. This was stated by al-Qadi and al-Zamakhshari.

There are many hadiths with the meaning of the verse, such as the hadith: "The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim; he does not wrong him nor forsake him." And the hadith: "Allah is in the aid of the servant as long as the servant is in the aid of his brother." And the hadith: "The likeness of the believers in their mutual affection, mercy, and kindness is like the likeness of one body: when a limb complains, the rest of the body responds to it with wakefulness and fever." And the hadith: "The believer to the believer is like a building, one part strengthening the other," and he (ﷺ) interlaced his fingers. All of these are in the (Sahih) collections.

﴿And fear Allah, that you may receive mercy﴾ means: be wary of opposing His judgment and of neglecting it, so that He may have mercy on you, forgiving your past sins and granting you His good pleasure.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[11] ﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people, perhaps they may be better than them; and not women [ridicule] women, perhaps they may be better than them. And do not defame one another or call each other by nicknames. Wretched is the name of disobedience after faith. And whoever does not repent, then it is those who are the wrongdoers.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people﴾: that is, let not men mock men, so that they regard themselves as better than those they mock. ﴿Perhaps they may be better than them; and not women [ridicule] women, perhaps they may be better than them﴾: that is, the women who mock.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The criterion of superiority in both groups is not what appears to people of forms, shapes, conditions and states, upon which the matter of ridicule generally turns. Rather, it is the matters hidden in the hearts. So no one should dare to belittle another, for perhaps that person is better than him in the sight of Allah, the Exalted, by virtue of what is bound to him of superiority, and so he wrongs himself by demeaning one whom Allah has honoured and by treating lightly one whom Allah has magnified. Among the interpreters are those who restricted ridicule to what occurs from the wealthy toward the poor, and others who restricted it to what happens when someone stumbles upon a slip or a lapse and then mocks him because of it.

al-Tabari said: The correct view is that Allah, by His prohibition to the believers that some of them mock others, has encompassed all the meanings of ridicule. It is not permissible for a believer to mock a believer, neither for his poverty, nor for a sin he committed, nor for anything else.

al-Ghazali (may Allah have mercy on him) counted ridicule among the afflictions of the tongue in (Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din), and he clarified its meaning in a way that leaves no further quest. We transmit it here to complete the benefit. He said, may Allah have mercy on him:

The eleventh affliction: ridicule and mockery. This is forbidden whatever its harm may be, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people﴾, and so on. The meaning of ridicule is treating lightly, belittling, and pointing out defects and deficiencies in a manner that provokes laughter. This may be by imitation in deed and speech, and it may be by gesture and signalling. If it occurs in the presence of the one mocked, it is not called backbiting, but it has the sense of backbiting.

"'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: I imitated someone, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to me: 'By Allah, I would not like to imitate a person, even if I were given such and such.'"

Ibn 'Abbas said regarding the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Woe to us! What is this book that leaves neither a small thing nor a great one but has enumerated it﴾ [al-Kahf: 49]: "The small thing is smiling at a believer in mockery, and the great thing is laughing outright at him."

This is an indication that laughing at people is among the major sins. Mu'adh ibn Jabal said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever reproaches his brother for a sin from which he has repented will not die until he commits it."

All of this returns to belittling another, laughing at him, treating him lightly, and considering him insignificant. This is what the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿perhaps they may be better than them﴾ alert to, that is: do not look down on him with contempt, for perhaps he is better than you. This prohibition applies only regarding one who is harmed by it. As for one who makes himself an object of mockery and perhaps rejoices at being mocked, then ridicule concerning him falls within jesting. Of it, some is blameworthy and some is praiseworthy. What is forbidden is only contemptuous treatment by which the one mocked is harmed, because of the belittling and disdain it contains. This happens at times by laughing at his speech when he stumbles in it and it is not coherent, or at his actions when they are disordered, such as laughing at his memorization or his craft, or at his appearance and build when he is short or deficient because of some defect. Laughing at all of these falls under the ridicule that is prohibited. End.

A subtle point:

Abu al-Su'ud said: "al-qawm" (people) is specific to men, because they are the managers over women. (The preferable reading is "al-muhimmat".) In origin it is either a plural of a participle, like "sawwam" and "zuwwar" as plurals of "sa'im" and "za'ir", or a verbal noun described by it which became common for the plural. As for its being used to include both groups, as in "the people of 'Ad" and "the people of Pharaoh", that is either by way of predominance (taghlib) or because the women are followers. The choice of the plural is because ridicule most often occurs in gatherings. The indefiniteness is either for generality, or intended to prohibit some of them from mocking others, since it is among what takes place between one and another.

﴿And do not defame one another﴾: that is, let not some of you find fault with others or slander them.

al-Shihab (al-Alusi) said: The pronoun in ﴿defame﴾ refers to the plural with an implied genitive construction. ﴿Yourselves﴾ is an expression for another part of the same kind as the addressees, namely the believers, so that what is of their kind is made equivalent to themselves, as in His words: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128], and His words: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29]. Thus "the selves" is used figuratively for the kind. In the noble expression there is therefore a figurative extension and an implied genitive. The prohibition on this reading is specific to the believers, and it is distinct from what precedes it, though it is also specific to the believers in terms of implication, since the defamation and ridicule differ. It cannot be said that the first renders the second redundant, for ridicule is mentioning someone with what he dislikes in a laughable manner in his presence, whereas this is mentioning him with what he dislikes in general. Or it is generalization after specification, as a general term is conjoined to a specific one to indicate comprehensiveness. It has also been said that it is conjunction of cause to effect, or that defamation is restricted to what is done in a covert manner, such as by gesture. Or it is conjunction of the specific to the general, treating the specific as another genus for the sake of emphasis. End.

It has also been said: the meaning of the verse is: do not do what you are defamed for, for whoever does what makes him deserving of defamation has defamed himself.

al-Shihab said: So "yourselves" is on its apparent sense, and the figurative element is in His words "defame". It is a metonymy in which the causer is mentioned and the cause is intended. The meaning is: do not commit an act for which you would be reproached. This is weakened on the grounds that it is far from the context and does not fit His words ﴿and do not call one another by nicknames﴾, as in al-Kashshaf. That it is figurative in the attribution, since what belongs to the causer is attributed to the cause, is an obvious strain. Likewise, that it is like a reason for the preceding prohibition does not remove its being contrary to the apparent sense. Likewise, that the intended meaning is: do not cause criticism of yourselves by criticizing others, as in the hadith: "Among the major sins is that a man curses his parents," which was explained as: when he curses the parents of another, the other curses his parents in return. End.

﴿And do not call one another by nicknames﴾: that is, do not call one another by nicknames which the one so named dislikes being called by. It has been narrated that it referred to a people who had names from the time of ignorance, and when they embraced Islam they became angry at being called by them. Narrated by Ahmad and Abu Dawud. Some of the early scholars (salaf) interpreted it as a man saying to another: "O sinner! O hypocrite!" and some as calling a man by disbelief after Islam, or by disobedience after repentance. The verse, as Ibn Jarir said, includes all of that. He said: Because mutual nickname-calling is calling a person by what he dislikes, whether a name or an attribute.

﴿Wretched is the name of disobedience after faith﴾. al-Zamakhshari said: "The name" here means the mention, from the expression: "his name flew among people for generosity or for baseness," as one says: "his praise and reputation flew." Its reality is what names him, his mention, and what rises among people. Do you not see the expression: "he raised his mention"? It is as if it were said: wretched is the mention that is raised for the believers because of committing these offences, that they be mentioned by disobedience. Regarding His words ﴿after faith﴾ there are three aspects:

(p-5461) One: the reprehensibility of combining faith with disobedience, which faith rejects and forbids, just as one says: "wretched is the affair after the staunchness, the frivolity."

The second: that in their insults toward those Jews who had embraced Islam they would say: "O Jew! O sinner!" and they were forbidden from it, and it was said to them: "Wretched is the mention, that you mention a man by disobedience and Judaism after his faith." The sentence on this interpretation is connected to the prohibition on nicknames.

The third: that it be taken as the disobedience of a non-believer, as one says to someone who turns from trade to farming: "Wretched is the craft, farming after trade." End.

Ibn Jarir chose the third, not in deference to the opinion of the Mu'tazilah that the disobedient person is not a believer, just as he is not a disbeliever, so that he occupies a position between the two positions, but because the context requires the speech to conclude with a threat. Calling someone by what people dislike is a blameworthy matter that does not combine with faith, for it is the emblem of the time of ignorance. His wording is: The Exalted One says: whoever does what We have forbidden, and commits disobedience to Us after his faith, and mocks the believers, and defames his believing brother, and calls him by nicknames, then he is a sinner: ﴿Wretched is the name of disobedience after faith﴾. He says: so do not do it, lest you deserve, if you do it, to be named sinners. Wretched is the name of disobedience. The statement of what we have described has been omitted, being sufficiently indicated by His words ﴿Wretched is the name of disobedience﴾. Then he weakened the second opinion and said: Other interpretations are more fitting to the speech, because Allah has already given the prohibition concerning what was forbidden at the beginning of this verse. The more appropriate course is to conclude it with a threat for whoever persists in transgression, or to make reprehensible the committing of what has been forbidden, not to report the ugliness of what the repentant person had done before his repentance, since the verse did not open with a report about committing ugly acts he had done before repentance, so that it would conclude with a threat for them. End.

﴿And whoever does not repent﴾: that is, from calling his brother by the nicknames Allah has forbidden to call him by, or from defaming him, or from mocking him. ﴿Then it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾: that is, those who wronged themselves by bringing upon themselves punishment through committing what they had been forbidden.

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 49, Verse 12

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[12] ﴿O you who have believed, avoid much [harmful] suspicion, for indeed, some suspicion is sin. And do not spy on one another, and do not backbite [ghiba] one another. Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his brother when he is dead? You would detest it. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance and Merciful.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, avoid much suspicion﴾ means: be cautious of it, i.e., keep away from it. This is by your thinking ill of people, for the one who suspects is not certain. The vagueness of "much" (al-kathir) is meant to make one cautious and scrupulous about the thoughts that stir in the hearts, since there is no motive that drives the believer to follow them or to dwell on them. Rather, it is a requirement of faith that believers think well of themselves. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think well of their own kind and say, "This is an obvious lie"?﴾ [al-Nur: 12]. Indeed, whoever openly displays his immorality and tears off his veil has made his honor permissible to people. Among what is related on this point is: "Whoever casts off the cloak of modesty, there is no backbiting about him." For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: "What distinguishes the suspicions that must be avoided from others is that every suspicion for which no sound indication and no apparent cause is known is forbidden and must be avoided. This applies when the person suspected is one who has been witnessed to be upright and righteous, and in whom trustworthiness has been observed outwardly. Then suspecting him of corruption and treachery is forbidden, unlike one whom people know to be engaged in dubious conduct and openly committing vile acts."

﴿Indeed, some suspicion﴾, which is the believer's suspicion of evil and not of good, ﴿is sin﴾, i.e., it earns punishment, because it involves committing what has been forbidden.

Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali said in (al-Ihya') in explaining the prohibition of backbiting by the heart: "Know that evil suspicion is forbidden, just as evil speech is. Just as it is forbidden for you to tell others with your tongue about the faults of others, it is not permitted for you to speak to yourself and think ill of your brother." He said: "I mean by it only the fixing of the heart upon it and judging others with evil suspicion. As for passing thoughts and inner talk, these are excused, and even doubt is excused. But what is forbidden is to suspect. Suspicion is an expression of what the soul relies upon and the heart inclines toward." Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿O you who have believed, avoid much suspicion; indeed, some suspicion is sin.﴾ He said: "The reason for its prohibition is that the secrets of hearts are known only to the Knower of the unseen. So you may not believe anything evil about others unless it becomes clear to you through direct witness that admits no interpretation. In that case you cannot help but believe what you have known and witnessed. But what you have not seen with your own eyes or heard with your own ears, and which has then occurred to your heart, it is only Satan who casts it to you. So you should reject it, even if the one concerned is the most profligate of sinners." Up to his saying: "Evil suspicion is not permitted except by that which permits taking someone's property, namely a directly witnessed sight or a just and reliable testimony." End of quotation.

Since spying is one of the fruits of evil suspicion, because the heart is not satisfied with suspicion and seeks certainty, so it occupies itself with spying, Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the prohibition of it immediately after evil suspicion. So He said: ﴿And do not spy.﴾ Ibn Jarir said: That is, let none of you pursue the nakedness [awra] of another, nor search out his inner secrets, seeking thereby to uncover his faults. Rather, be content with what has become apparent to you of his affairs, and by that praise or blame him, not by what you know of his inner secrets.

It is said: "Tajassasa al-amr" means he sought it out and investigated it, like "talammasa." Al-Shihab said: "Al-jass" (with a jim) is like al-lams (touching); it carries the meaning of seeking, because whoever seeks something touches it and feels it. So the word is used for what this entails, and the form tafa''ala is used for emphasis."

Al-Ghazali said: "The meaning of tajassus is that one does not leave the servants of Allah under the cover of Allah, but seeks to reach a point of looking in and tearing away the veil, until what was hidden from him becomes exposed to him. Leaving them be is more secure for one's heart and religion."

(p-5464) Many hadiths have been related about the meaning of this verse, among them the hadith that "the Prophet (ﷺ) gave a sermon and raised his voice until he made the young women in their chambers hear him, and he said: 'O assembly of those who have believed with their tongues while faith has not entered their hearts! Do not follow the faults of the Muslims, for whoever follows the faults of the Muslims, Allah will follow his fault until He disgraces him, even within his own house.'"

In the Sahih (of al-Bukhari and Muslim) it is related from him (ﷺ): "Do not spy, do not search for information about one another [tahassus], do not hate one another, do not turn away from one another, and be, O servants of Allah, brothers." Abu Dawud related that Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, was brought a man, and it was said to him: "This is so-and-so, his beard is dripping with wine!" He said: "We have been forbidden from spying, but if something becomes apparent to us, we will act upon it." The man was named by Ibn Abi Hatim in his narration: al-Walid ibn Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt.

Abu Dawud related from Mu'awiya who said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: 'If you follow the faults of people, you will corrupt them, or you will nearly corrupt them.'" Then Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him, said a word that Mu'awiya heard from the Messenger of Allah, and Allah benefited him by it.

Imam Ahmad related "from Dujayn, the scribe of Uqba, who said to Uqba: 'We have neighbors who drink wine, and I call the police to them so they can seize them!' He said: 'Do not do that, but admonish them and threaten them!' He said: So he did, but they did not desist. He said: Then Dujayn came to him and said: 'I admonished them, but they did not desist, and I call the police to them so you can seize them!' Uqba said to him: 'Do not do that, for I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever conceals the fault of a believer is as if he has saved a girl buried alive from her grave."'"

Abu Dawud related from Abu Umama, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "If the ruler seeks out suspicion among the people, he corrupts them." Al-Awza'i said: "Included in spying is listening to a people who dislike it."

﴿And do not backbite one another﴾, i.e., let none of you say about another in his absence what the one spoken of would dislike to be said to his face. It is said: "Ghaba-hu" and "ightabahu," like "ghala-hu" and "ightalahu," when one mentions him with evil in his absence. ﴿Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his brother when he is dead? You would detest it.﴾ That is, if it were presented to you, your souls would recoil from it and you would detest it. Therefore you should detest backbiting. Here there is an allegorical metaphor [isti'ara tamthiliyya], likening one person's backbiting of another to eating the flesh of a dead brother.

Lata'if (subtle points):

The first: Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿Would one of you like...﴾ etc. is an illustration and depiction of what the backbiter takes from the honor of the person he backbites, in the most dreadful and vile manner. In it are various intensifications. Among them: the interrogative, whose meaning is affirmation, which conveys emphasis in that it never occurs in the speech of a Muslim in the hearing of anyone, literally or as a supplication. Among them: placing what is the ultimate of disliking in conjunction with liking. Among them: attributing the verb to 'one of you' and conveying that neither of the two would like that. Among them: that the depiction of backbiting is not confined to eating the flesh of a human being, but makes the human being a brother. Among them: that it is not confined to eating the flesh of a brother, but he is made dead." End of quotation.

Ibn al-Athir said in (al-Mathal al-Sa'ir), in the section on kinaya [metonymy/allusion]: "Among this is His saying: ﴿Would one of you like...﴾ etc., for He alluded to backbiting by eating the flesh of a human being, the flesh of another human like him. Then He did not stop there until He made him dead. Then He placed what is the ultimate of disliking in conjunction with liking. These are four indications, each corresponding to what it was intended for, matching the meaning for which it was revealed.

As for making backbiting like eating the flesh of a human being, the flesh of another human like him, it is extremely fitting, because backbiting is nothing but mentioning people's faults and tearing their honor apart. Tearing honor is similar to a person eating the flesh of the one he backbites, because eating flesh is literal tearing. As for making it like the flesh of a brother, it is because of the detestation inherent in backbiting, since both reason and the Shari'a agree in loathing it and command abstaining from it and keeping away from it. Since it is like that, it was made equivalent to the flesh of a brother in being detested.

It is known that human flesh is loathsome to another human, yet it is not like the loathing of one's brother's flesh. So this expression is an intensification in making backbiting loathsome. As for placing what is the ultimate of disliking in conjunction with liking, it is because of what souls have been created to incline toward backbiting and to crave it, along with knowing its ugliness. Consider, O reflective one, this kinaya, and you will find it among the most closely matching of allusions, for when you look at each of those four indications we have pointed out, you will find each one fitting what it was intended for." End of quotation.

The second: The fa' in His saying ﴿so you detested it﴾ is fa' fasiha [a connecting particle implying an unstated condition], answering an implied condition. The meaning: "If that is true, or if this is presented to you, then you have detested it." What is mentioned is the answer to the condition, and it is in the past tense, so "qad" is implicitly understood with it, so that the fa' can enter upon the past-tense answer, as in His saying: ﴿So they have denied you with what you say﴾ [al-Furqan: 19]. The pronoun in ﴿fakarihtumuhu﴾ refers to the eating, and it has been permitted that it refers to the backbiting understood from it. The meaning: "So detest it, the way you detest that eating." It was expressed in the past tense for emphasis. When it is interpreted as mentioned, it becomes performative [insha'i] and does not require the implicit "qad," as al-Shihab noted.

The third: Ibn al-Faras said: "From the verse it is deduced that it is not permissible for one compelled by necessity to eat the carrion of a human being, because it was used as the example in the prohibition of backbiting, and it was not used as the example for the carrion of other animals. So this indicates that in prohibition it is above them. Whoever wishes to exhaust the topics of backbiting should consult (al-Ihya') of al-Ghazali, for he gathered and comprehended."

﴿And fear Allah﴾, i.e., be wary of His punishment by refraining from what He has forbidden you of evil suspicion, spying on what is concealed, backbiting, and the other prohibitions. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance and Merciful﴾, i.e., He accepts the repentance of those who turn back to Him, and bestows His mercy by sparing them punishment after their return.

Then, after His prohibition of backbiting and of people belittling one another, Exalted is He alerted [to the fact] that they are equal in humanity, as Ibn Kathir said, with His words, glorified is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 49, verse 13:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[13] ﴿O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female and made you peoples (shu'ub) and tribes (qaba'il) that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Acquainted.﴾

﴿O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female﴾ means: from Adam and Eve, or from the semen of a male among the men and the semen of a female among the women. That is, from a father and a mother. None of you is other than one who traces his lineage to the same origin as the other, equal to equal. So there is no basis for boasting or for preference in lineage.

﴿And made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another﴾ Ibn Jarir said: And We made you related to one another, so some of you are related to others through a distant lineage, and some of you are related to others through a close lineage, so that some of you may know others through the nearness or distance of kinship with them, not for any virtue you possess in that, nor for any nearness that brings you closer to Allah. Rather, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾, that is, the one most mindful of Him and most fearful of Him in performing His obligations and avoiding His disobediences, not the one with the greatest house or the most numerous kin.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Acquainted﴾ that is: of your outward and inward states, of the most righteous and the most noble, and of other than that. Nothing hidden is concealed from Him.

Remarks:

The first: Al-Tha'alibi, in (Fiqh al-Lugha), relating the gradation of the tribe from the greater to the lesser, transmitted from Ibn al-Kalbi, from his father, that the sha'b (with a fatha on the shin) is greater than the qabila, then the qabila, then the 'imara (with a kasra on the ayn), then the batn, then the fakhdh. And from another: the sha'b, then the qabila, then the fasila, then the 'ashira, then the dhurriyya, then the 'itra, then the usra. End of quotation. Shaykh Ibn Barri said: The correct ordering in this is what al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar arranged, which is: the sha'b, then the qabila, then the 'imara, then the batn, then the fakhdh, then the fasila. Abu Usama said: These levels are in the order of the creation of man. So the sha'b is the greatest of them, derived from sha'b al-ra's (the crown/side of the head). Then the qabila, from qabilat al-ra's (the top of the head) because they gather together. Then the 'imara, which is the chest. Then the batn (the belly). Then the fakhdh (the thigh). Then the fasila, which is the shin. Some added the 'ashira, and said:

I intend the sha'b, for it is the largest living group in number, within the 'hiwa', then the qabila.
Then follows it the 'imara, then the batn, and after it the fakhdh and the fasila.
Then after them the 'ashira, but it is, compared with what we have mentioned, a small thing.

So Khuzayma is a sha'b, Kinana is a qabila, Quraysh is an 'imara, Qusayy is a batn, Hashim is a fakhdh, and al-Abbas is a fasila. The (shu'ub) were so named because the tribes branched out (tasha''abat) from them. And (shu'ub) is the plural of sha'b, with a fatha on the shin.

Abu Ubayd al-Bakri said in (Sharh Nawadir Abi Ali al-Qali): All the transmitters related the sha'b for a tribe with a fatha, and for a mountain with a kasra, except Bundar, for he transmitted it from Abu Ubayda in the reverse. Al-Zabidi transmitted this in (Taj al-Arus).

The second: The verse indicates the concern with lineages, that they were legislated for recognition, and the condemnation of boasting by them, and that the righteous person, even if not of noble descent, is preferred over the noble descent who is not righteous. Thus the one who is excellent in leadership (imama) is preferred over the noble descent who is neither of these two.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Wahb who said: I asked Malik about marrying the non-Arab clients (mawali) to Arab women. He said: It is permitted. Then he recited this verse. He did not stipulate freedom (hurriyya) as a condition of equality in marriage (kafa'a). This was transmitted in (al-Iklil).

Ibn Kathir said: Those who held that equality (kafa'a) in marriage is not a condition, and that nothing is required beyond religion, took evidence from the verse.

The third: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that you may know one another﴾ indicates a restriction (hasr) of the wisdom of making them peoples and tribes to this. That is: We made you thus only so that some of you may know others, so that you maintain the ties of kinship, distinguish lineages, and inheritance, not for boasting by fathers and tribes.

Al-Shihab said: The restriction is derived from the specification by mention and the silence within the context of explanation. Al-Qashani said: The meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ is that there is no nobility by lineage, since all are equal in the humanity that traces back to a male and a female. Distinction by peoples and tribes exists only for the sake of recognition through kinship, not for boasting, for that is one of the vices. Nobility is not attained except by abstaining from vices, which is the root of righteousness. Then, whenever righteousness is greater in rank, its possessor is more noble in the sight of Allah and greater in station. So the one who refrains from the prohibitions of the Sharia, which are sins, in the customary sense of the outward Sharia, is more noble than the wicked person. And the one who refrains from ethical vices such as ignorance, stinginess, greed, covetousness, and cowardice is more noble than the one who avoids sins but is characterized by them. End of quotation.

The fourth: Many hadiths have been related regarding the meaning of the verse. Among them is what al-Bukhari related from Abu Hurayra who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: Who is the most noble of people? He said: The most noble of them in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of them. They said: We are not asking you about this. He said: Then the most noble of people is Yusuf, the Prophet of Allah, son of the Prophet of Allah, son of the Prophet of Allah, son of the Friend of Allah. They said: We are not asking you about this. He said: Then are you asking me about the sources (ma'adin) of the Arabs? They said: Yes. He said: Then the best of you in the Jahiliyya are the best of you in Islam, when they gain understanding.

Muslim also related from him: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Indeed Allah does not look at your forms and your wealth, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds.

Imam Ahmad related from Abu Dhar who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: Look, for you are not better than a red man nor a black man, except that you surpass him in piety toward Allah.

Al-Bazzar related in his Musnad from Hudhayfa, from the Prophet (ﷺ): All of you are the children of Adam, and Adam was created from dust. Let people cease boasting of their forefathers, or they will be more contemptible in the sight of Allah, exalted is He, than the dung beetles.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Umar that the Prophet (ﷺ) said in his sermon on the day of the Conquest of Mecca: O people! Indeed Allah, exalted is He, has removed from you the arrogance of the Jahiliyya and its glorification of forefathers. People are of two kinds: a righteous, pious man who is noble in the sight of Allah, exalted is He, and a wicked man who is feared, contemptible in the sight of Allah, exalted is He. Indeed Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female﴾, the verse.

Other hadiths remain, which Ibn Kathir cited, so refer to them.

Al-Tabari related from Ata who said: Ibn Abbas said: There are three verses which people have denied: the permission entirely, and His saying ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾, and people said: The most noble of you is the one greatest in house. Ata said: I have forgotten the third.

Since the opening of the surah concerns the coarse Bedouins and the denunciation of their bad morals, and then their being affected by the prohibitions against the reprehensible acts that abound among them, and since they were the primary and direct target, and then secondarily and indirectly others, the surah concludes by defining that whoever is of their likeness in committing those prohibited acts is among those in whose heart faith has not entered. Then it explains who the true believer is, so that they may understand that the matter is not as they claim. Thus, glorified and exalted is He, said:

(p-5471)

The discussion of the words of His, the Exalted:

[14] ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; but say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts. And if you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not deprive you of anything of your deeds. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."﴾
